title: CS161 13: SQL Injection, the Web and Same-Origin Policy

questions.q: A calculator website passes whatever the user types straight into Python's `eval` on the server. What is the core reason this is dangerous?
choices: eval is slow, so long expressions let an attacker cause a denial of service
User input becomes part of the code the server runs, so a crafted input can make the server execute unintended code
eval prints the server's source code back to the user
eval only accepts numbers, so non-numeric input crashes the server
questions.explain: This is code injection: unchecked input gets interpreted as code. An input that closes the expression and appends something like `os.system(...)` could make the server run any command, such as deleting its files.

questions.q: What is the relationship between SQL injection and code injection?
choices: They are unrelated: code injection targets browsers and SQL injection targets servers
Code injection is a special case of SQL injection
SQL injection is a special case of code injection, where the injected code is SQL run by the database
SQL injection can only read data, while code injection can only modify data
questions.explain: Both work the same way: the server builds code (here, a SQL query) out of user input, and crafted input changes what that code does.

questions.q: A server builds `SELECT rating FROM evals WHERE course = '<input>'`. An attacker submits `garbage'; SELECT password FROM passwords WHERE username = 'admin`. What does the single quote right after `garbage` do?
choices: It starts a SQL comment so the rest of the original query is ignored
It closes the string opened by the original query, so the text after it is parsed as SQL code instead of string data
It ends the first query so a second query can begin
It escapes the semicolon so the server doesn't notice it
questions.explain: Without that quote, everything the attacker typed would stay inside the course-name string. The `;` is what ends the first query.

questions.q: A server builds `SELECT rating FROM evals WHERE course = '<input>'`. The attacker's input `garbage'; SELECT password FROM passwords WHERE username = 'admin` has no closing quote after `admin`. Why?
choices: The original query template adds a quote after the input, which completes `'admin'`
SQL string literals at the end of a query don't need a closing quote
A closing quote would be escaped by the server
The `;` earlier in the input already closed all strings
questions.explain: The template wraps the input in quotes. The template's own closing quote ends up right after `admin`, so the result is valid SQL. An extra quote from the attacker would leave an unmatched quote.

questions.q: In the injection `garbage'; SELECT password FROM passwords WHERE username = 'admin` against `SELECT rating FROM evals WHERE course = '<input>'`, why does the input start with a junk value like `garbage` instead of a real course name?
choices: So the database raises an error that reveals the table structure
Because the server rejects inputs that match real course names
So the semicolon is treated as part of the string
So the intended query returns nothing and doesn't get mixed into the attacker's results
questions.explain: The first, intended query gets a value that matches no rows, so only the attacker's query returns anything useful.

questions.q:
A login page runs `SELECT username FROM users WHERE username = '' AND password = '

'` and logs you in if any rows come back. You enter username `alice' OR 1=1--` and password `garbage`. Why does this log you in?
choices: `OR 1=1` is always true, so the WHERE clause matches every row, and `--` comments out the password check and the leftover quote
`1=1` sets alice's password to 1, which the password comparison then matches
`--` deletes alice's password, so any password is accepted
The query fails with a syntax error, and the server treats errors as successful logins
questions.explain: The query becomes `... WHERE username = 'alice' OR 1=1--' AND password = 'garbage'`. Everything after `--` is a comment, and `OR 1=1` makes the condition true for every row, so more than 0 rows come back.

questions.q: The `' OR 1=1--` login bypass only works if the attacker knows at least one valid username.
questions.explain: `1=1` is true for every row, so the query returns rows whether or not the username before it exists. The login check only needs more than 0 rows.

questions.q: Which two-character sequence starts a comment in SQL, so the parser ignores the rest of the query?
questions.explain: Attackers append `--` so leftover parts of the original query (closing quotes, password checks) are ignored.

questions.q: After breaking out of the string in an injected login query, the leftover original text (e.g. `' AND password = '...'`) must not cause a syntax error. Which techniques deal with that leftover text?
choices: Append `--` so the rest of the query is treated as a comment
Append `;` and then a dummy query whose ending matches the remaining original SQL
Append `OR 1=1`
Start the input with a junk value
questions.explain: A comment hides the leftover SQL, and `;` plus a dummy query turns it into the end of a valid second statement. `OR 1=1` only makes rows come back, and a junk value only keeps the intended query empty. Neither fixes the trailing syntax.

questions.q: What does it mean to escape a character in input that goes into a SQL query?
choices: Remove the character from the input
Mark the character so SQL treats it as a literal part of the string instead of SQL syntax
Encrypt the character so the database can't read it
Reject the whole request if the character appears
questions.explain: For example, an escaped quote doesn't end the current string, so malicious input stays string data and the parser never runs it as SQL.

questions.q:
A server escapes every `'` and `-` in user input before building `SELECT username FROM users WHERE username = '' AND password = '

'`. An attacker enters username `alice' OR 1=1--`. What happens?
choices: The login succeeds because `OR 1=1` is still evaluated
The quote is neutralized, but the `--` comment still takes effect
The database looks for a user whose name is literally `alice' OR 1=1--` and finds nothing
The query errors out because escaped characters aren't allowed in SQL
questions.explain: The escaped quote doesn't end the username string and the escaped dashes don't start a comment, so the whole input is just a strange username.

questions.q: A homemade escaper replaces each `'` with `\'`. An attacker types `\'` (a backslash then a quote), and the escaper outputs `\\'`. Why can the attacker still break out of the string?
choices: The parser reads `\\` as one escaped backslash, so the quote after it is unescaped and ends the string
Escaping the quote twice cancels out and turns it into a comment
The parser drops all backslashes in front of quotes
They can't. Doubled backslashes always make the quote literal
questions.explain: The escaper only escaped the quote, not the attacker's backslash. The two backslashes pair up as a literal backslash, leaving a real quote. Edge cases like this are why you shouldn't write your own escaper.

questions.q: How do parameterized SQL / prepared statements stop SQL injection?
choices: They automatically escape quotes and dashes before building the query string
They reject any input containing SQL keywords like SELECT or OR
They run every query read-only so injected writes fail
The query is compiled and parsed first and user input is plugged in afterward, so input can never be read as SQL code
questions.explain: The query's structure is fixed before the input arrives, so no input can change what the query does.

questions.q: Parameterized SQL prevents all SQL injection attacks.
questions.explain: User input is added only after the query has been parsed, so it is always treated as data and never as SQL. That makes parameterized SQL the best defense.

questions.q: What is the main drawback of parameterized SQL?
choices: It is slower than escaping because every query is compiled twice
Compatibility: it needs support from the database itself and has no common standard, which can make switching databases harder
It only protects SELECT queries, not INSERT or UPDATE
It still lets attackers inject comments with `--`
questions.explain: Plain SQL is mostly portable across databases, but parameterization is processed on the database side with no shared syntax. Libraries usually handle the translation.

questions.q: Even with a correct escaper from a well-tested SQL library, why is escaping often an ineffective defense in a codebase that builds SQL from raw user input?
choices: Every single query must be escaped correctly, and one missed call leaves a vulnerability
Library escapers are always broken by the backslash-quote trick
Escaped input can't be stored in the database
Escaping only works for GET requests, not POST requests
questions.explain: Escaping depends on never forgetting it anywhere. Parameterized SQL is far more robust.

questions.q: A team wants to rule out SQL injection in its application, but its SQL library doesn't support parameterized queries. What's the best approach?
choices: Write a custom escaper tailored to their database
Strip the words SELECT, OR and DROP from all input
Switch to a SQL library that supports parameterized SQL, then replace every query call with the parameterized API
Send every query through a POST request
questions.explain: Most modern libraries support parameterized SQL, and safe and unsafe queries use separate API functions. Finding every query and switching it to the parameterized call removes the whole class of bugs.

questions.q: When you do need to escape SQL input, writing your own escaper is better than using your SQL library's, because you can tailor it to your queries.
questions.explain: Building a correct escaper is tricky and full of edge cases. Secure escapers already exist in SQL libraries for almost every language.

questions.q: In `https://bob@shop.example.com:8443/cart/view?item=42&qty=3#reviews`, what is the path?
choices: `shop.example.com/cart/view`
`/cart/view`
`/cart/view?item=42&qty=3`
`/cart/view?item=42&qty=3#reviews`
questions.explain: The path starts at the first single slash after the location and ends before the `?` parameters.

questions.q: In `https://bob@shop.example.com:8443/cart/view?item=42&qty=3#reviews`, what is the port number?
questions.explain: The port follows the domain after a colon, as part of the location.

questions.q: When the browser fetches `https://shop.example.com/cart/view?item=42&qty=3#reviews`, which part is NOT sent to the web server?
choices: `reviews` (the anchor)
`item=42&qty=3` (the parameters)
`/cart/view` (the path)
`shop.example.com` (the domain)
questions.explain: The anchor stays in the browser. The page can read it, and it's often used to scroll to a section. The parameters and path go to the server, and the domain is sent in the Host header.

questions.q: Which parts are mandatory in every URL?
choices: Protocol (scheme)
Location (domain)
Path
Port
Query parameters
Anchor
Username
questions.explain: Port, parameters, anchor and username are all optional. The path can be as short as `/`.

questions.q: What does the protocol (scheme) part of a URL tell the browser?
choices: Which web server to contact
Which resource on the server to request
How to retrieve the resource
Where on the page to scroll
questions.explain: Examples are `http`, `https`, `ftp` and `git+ssh`. The location says which server to contact, and the path says which resource to request.

questions.q: Which part of a URL does the web server use to decide which page or resource to return?
choices: The protocol
The anchor
The username
The path
questions.explain: The path works like a file path on the server, starting from the root `/`.

questions.q: Why might a URL's location include a port number, as in `www.example.com:81`?
choices: To distinguish between different applications running on the same web server
To choose which file on the server to return
To tell the browser to use an encrypted connection
To identify the user making the request
questions.explain: One machine can run several services, and the port says which one to talk to.

questions.q: What is the shortest possible path in a URL (the root of the site's filesystem)?
questions.explain: The path must contain at least `/`. It's called the root because the filesystem is a tree that starts there.

questions.q: In a URL, which character starts the parameters and which character separates them from each other?
choices: `#` starts them and `&` separates them
`?` starts them and `&` separates them
`?` starts them and `;` separates them
`&` starts them and `?` separates them
questions.explain: For example, `?k1=v1&k2=v2`. Each parameter is usually a `key=value` pair.

questions.q: In HTTP's request-response model, how does an exchange begin?
choices: The server pushes pages to clients as soon as the pages change
The client (e.g. a browser) opens a connection to the server and sends a request, and the server answers it
Client and server send requests to each other at the same time
The server opens a connection to the client once it learns the client's address
questions.explain: Clients must actively start the connection and issue a request. The server sends a response to every request.

questions.q: The first line of an HTTP request is `POST /login HTTP/1.1`. What are its three parts, in order?
choices: Method, path, protocol version
Path, method, host
Method, host, content type
Protocol, domain, path
questions.explain: `POST` is the method, `/login` is the path, and `HTTP/1.1` is the protocol version. Header lines come after it.

questions.q: In an HTTP request, the lines right after the first line (e.g. `Host: squigler.com`, `Dnt: 1`) are:
choices: Query parameters
The request body
Request headers
Response headers
questions.explain: Each line after the request line is a header carrying metadata about the request. In a POST request, the body comes after the headers.

questions.q: Which HTTP method is meant for sending information that changes the server's state, such as posting a forum comment or changing a password?
choices: GET
POST
Either one. HTTP doesn't intend any difference
questions.explain: GET is meant for getting information. POST is meant for sending data that modifies the server's internal state.

questions.q: Of GET and POST, only POST requests can carry a body. A GET request passes data through query parameters in the URL instead.
questions.explain: For example, `GET /posts?search=security&sortby=popularity` sends two parameters in the URL, while a POST login sends `username=...&password=...` in its body.

questions.q: Because HTTP's original model says GET requests shouldn't change server state, modern web applications never change state in response to a GET request.
questions.explain: The original model intended that, but modern web applications often do change server state based on GET query parameters.

questions.q: How does HTTP2 differ from HTTP 1.1?
choices: HTTP2 adds encryption, which HTTP 1.1 lacks
HTTP2 drops headers and sends only payloads
HTTP2 lets servers open connections to clients
HTTP 1.1 is text-based, while HTTP2 is binary-encoded for efficiency. The same concepts of headers and payloads apply
questions.explain: Both versions use requests and responses made of headers plus a payload. Only the encoding differs.

questions.q: What is HTTPS?
choices: A secure version of HTTP that runs over TLS
HTTP that uses only POST requests
The binary-encoded version of HTTP
HTTP with the username included in the URL
questions.explain: HTTPS is HTTP over TLS. The binary-encoded version is HTTP2, which is a different thing.

questions.q: HTTP can return any kind of file. How does the browser know whether a response body is an HTML page, an image or a PDF?
choices: From the anchor in the URL
It always assumes HTML
A media type in the response header tells it how to interpret the body
From the request method used
questions.explain: The response header usually specifies a media type, such as an HTML or image type.

questions.q: A modern web page can be thought of as a distributed application. What does that mean?
choices: Part of it runs on the web server, which builds the HTTP response, and part runs in the browser, which processes the response and displays it
It is loaded from several servers at once for redundancy
Each user's browser shares computation with other users' browsers
Its HTML, CSS and JavaScript must come from different domains
questions.explain: The browser sends a request, the server computes and sends a response, and then the browser computes on that response and shows the result.

questions.q: Which HTML tag embeds an entire other web page inside the current page?
questions.explain: For example, `<iframe src="http://cs161.org"></iframe>`. Frames are risky because the inner page may come from a different, possibly malicious source.

questions.q: What does frame isolation guarantee when a page embeds another page in a frame?
choices: The inner page can't run JavaScript
The outer page can read the inner page but not modify it
The outer page can't change the inner page's contents, and the inner page can't change the outer page's contents
The inner page must come from the same domain as the outer page
questions.explain: Modern browsers enforce this in both directions, because the embedded page might be malicious, or the page embedding it might be.

questions.q: If an attacker can force a victim's browser to load malicious CSS, that's functionally as bad as forcing it to load malicious JavaScript.
questions.explain: Used maliciously, CSS is as powerful as JavaScript, even though it looks like it only controls fonts, colors and spacing.

questions.q: In what order does a browser process an HTML document?
choices: Render the HTML, then run JavaScript on the rendered output
Convert the HTML into the DOM, apply JavaScript to the DOM, then render the DOM
Run JavaScript first, turn its output into HTML, then build the DOM
Convert the HTML into CSS, then into JavaScript, then render
questions.explain: The DOM (Document Object Model) is the browser's internal form of the page. JavaScript changes the DOM, and then the browser renders it.

questions.q: In general, JavaScript on a page can arbitrarily modify any of that page's HTML or CSS.
questions.explain: JavaScript is very powerful, and that is why browsers sandbox it from the rest of your computer and from other pages.

questions.q: Why do browsers run JavaScript in a sandbox?
choices: To make JavaScript run faster through Just In Time compilation
To stop JavaScript from changing the page's HTML and CSS
To stop JavaScript from making any HTTP requests
So code loaded from a web page can't access sensitive data on your computer or data on other web pages
questions.explain: JavaScript can freely change its own page. The sandbox keeps it from reaching outside that page.

questions.q: Why do most exploits that target the web browser itself need JavaScript?
choices: The vulnerability is often in the browser's JavaScript engine
JavaScript can shape the program's memory layout to make the attack more likely to succeed
JavaScript is the only language that can make HTTP requests
JavaScript runs outside the browser's sandbox
questions.explain: Either the bug is in the JavaScript engine, or JavaScript is used to arrange memory so a memory-safety exploit works reliably. JavaScript does run inside a sandbox.

questions.q: How do almost all web browsers run JavaScript?
choices: Line-by-line interpretation with no compilation
Just In Time compilation into machine code
Ahead-of-time compilation on the web server
By sending it to the server to run and showing the result
questions.explain: Browsers convert JavaScript into machine code dynamically, because running JavaScript fast matters so much.

questions.q: You have `www.evil.com` open in one tab and your webmail in another. What does the same-origin policy prevent?
choices: The evil page reading your emails or sending emails as you through the webmail page
The evil page being loaded at all
Network eavesdroppers seeing your traffic to the evil site
The webmail page running any JavaScript
questions.explain: The browser isolates pages from each other unless they have the same origin, so the evil page can't touch the webmail page.

questions.q: Which components determine a web page's origin?
choices: Protocol
Domain name
Port
Path
Query parameters
Username
questions.explain: Origin = protocol + domain + port. Paths are not checked.

questions.q: How does the same-origin policy decide whether two pages share an origin?
choices: It checks whether both domains resolve to the same IP address
It treats a subdomain as the same origin as its parent domain
It compares the two sites' TLS certificates
Exact string matching on protocol, domain and port
questions.explain: All three must match exactly. That's why `example.com` and `www.example.com` are different origins.

questions.q: Which pair of URLs has the same origin?
choices: `http://example.com` and `http://www.example.com`
`https://shop.example.com/cart` and `https://shop.example.com:443/checkout?id=5`
`http://example.com` and `https://example.com`
`http://example.com:8080` and `http://example.com:8081`
questions.explain: Both are https with domain shop.example.com, and https defaults to port 443. Paths and parameters don't matter. The other pairs differ in domain, protocol or port.

questions.q: `http://example.com/a` and `http://example.com:80/b` have the same origin.
questions.explain: http defaults to port 80, so the ports match. The protocol and domain match too, and paths aren't checked.

questions.q: Do `https://example.com` and `https://example.com:80` have the same origin?
choices: Yes: the protocol and domain match, and the port is ignored
Yes: 80 is the default port for every protocol
No: with no port given, https defaults to 443, which doesn't match 80
No: the second URL has no path
questions.explain: Default ports are 80 for http and 443 for https. The first URL is effectively port 443.

questions.q: When an `https` URL doesn't specify a port, what port number is assumed when comparing origins?
questions.explain: https defaults to port 443, and http defaults to port 80.

questions.q: A page at `http://news.example` includes `<script src="http://ads.tracker.com/t.js"></script>`. What origin does that script run with?
choices: `http://ads.tracker.com`, where it was fetched from
`http://news.example`, the page that loads it
None. Scripts from other domains are blocked
Both origins at once
questions.explain: JavaScript runs with the origin of the page that loads it, not the origin it was downloaded from. Including a third-party script gives it full access as your page.

questions.q: A page at `http://news.example` embeds `<iframe src="https://mail.example.com"></iframe>`. What origin does the frame have?
choices: `https://mail.example.com`, the URL it was retrieved from
`http://news.example`, the page that embeds it
`http://mail.example.com`, because the outer page uses http
None until the user interacts with it
questions.explain: Frames take the origin of the URL they load, not the origin of the page embedding them. Scripts are the opposite.

questions.q: A page at `http://news.example` loads an image from `http://photos.example.net/cat.jpg`. Which statement is true?
choices: The image takes the origin `http://news.example`, so the page can read its pixels
The image is blocked because it comes from a different origin
The image has no origin
The image has the origin `http://photos.example.net`, and the loading page only learns its dimensions
questions.explain: Images keep the origin they come from. The page that embeds the image can display it but only knows its dimensions.

questions.q: How can two pages from different origins communicate in a controlled way?
choices: By embedding each other in frames, which lets each edit the other's DOM
By loading each other's scripts, which merges their origins
Through JavaScript's `postMessage` function, which allows only limited functionality
They can't communicate at all
questions.explain: `postMessage` is the special exception for cross-origin communication. Frame isolation stops frames from editing each other.
